scenes.text: Hey everyone, Professor Alienstein here! Big news from your planet. A NASA space telescope just fell out of the sky! How does something float up there for twenty-two years, and then suddenly come down?
Meet Swift. It was launched in two thousand four, and it hunted gamma ray bursts, some of the biggest explosions in the universe. It was only built to work for two years. It worked for twenty-two!
So how does a satellite stay up? Here's the secret. It is actually falling all the time. It just moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing the ground!
But up there, space is not totally empty. There is a very, very thin layer of air. It is tiny, but it pushes on the satellite like a slow, invisible brake. Scientists call it drag.
And here's the twist. The Sun was extra active lately. That heats the upper air and makes it puff up, like a balloon. So there was more drag, and Swift sank faster than planned.

cues.arg: Active Sun>Air puffs up>More drag>Orbit sinks

scenes.big: CAN'T WE JUST PUSH IT UP?
scenes.text: Why didn't NASA just push it back up? Swift has no engine to climb higher, and a private rescue mission that launched in July did not manage to lift it.

cues.arg: Swift=Has no engine|Rescue=A private robot tried in July

scenes.text: On November fourth, Swift came down over Indonesia. At that speed, the air squeezes and heats up, and most of the telescope burns up. NASA estimated about a one in two thousand one hundred chance that any surviving pieces would land in a populated area. So no need to panic!

cues.arg: Super fast speed>Air squeezes>Huge heat>Burns up

scenes.text: Swift gave us twenty-two years of discoveries. And experts say satellites without engines need a plan for how their story ends. Which strange space thing should I explain next? Tell me in the comments. See you soon!
